newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA'S SOCIALISTS SEEK CABINET DESPITE PROTEST.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA'S SOCIALISTS SEEK CABINET DESPITE PROTEST.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists, spurning 27 days of opposition protests to demand elections, will go ahead with plans to form a new government next week.
"I'm sure next week Bulgaria will have a new government but it is hard to predict what the future of this government will be," Socialist party leader Georgi Parvanov said.
Nikolai Dobrev, nominated to form the government, would be prime minister if the cabinet wins the approval of the 240-seat parliament, he said in a television interview on Saturday.

Students and the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) have vowed to intensify their protests, and disrupt road and rail links further, if the Socialists form a new government instead of opting for immediate elections.
Bulgaria has had a caretaker cabinet, unable to act on a deep economic crisis, since December when prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned.
Parvanov said the Socialists could count on 122 votes in parliament, less than their 125 seats but an absolute majority and able to win the required confidence vote.

"I think that the anti-crisis programme which is proposed by Nikolai Dobrev is quite constructive but will still need about 30 to 40 days to implement and to regain the confidence of the people," Parvanov added.
He said Bulgaria must have a government immediately to pass legislation to stop the collapse of the lev and inflation at 50 percent a month. The government must also pass the 1997 budget.
The Socialists have said they would hold general elections, due in December 1998, later this year but this offer has failed to satisfy the opposition, which wants the vote held now.
The Socialists -- Bulgaria's former communists -- will hold a special session on Sunday grouping their parliamentary deputies, coalition partners and the party's supreme council.

The session is expected to choose the ministers for the new cabinet. For the past week there have been signs of splits and a reluctunce by some party members to join the cabinet in view of such widespread popular opposition.
Thousands of students, workers and opposition supporters have staged daily nationwide rallies to demand the Socialists quit, blaming them for the economic collapse.
Festive protesters streamed through Sofia on Saturday on the 27th day of anti-government rallies, blowing horns, banging drums and carrying banners proclaiming "I am not a slave".
Students, families and pensioners poured in to the square at Alexander Nevski Orthodox cathedral to hear popular bands belt out tunes and opposition leaders whip up support.
"We think that victory is very close," UFD leader Ivan Kostov told a cheering throng hours before Parvanov expressed his determination to have a new Socialist government.

Several thousand UDF supporters blocked road and rail links to Greece for a fourth day. About 100 riot police stood nearby while tyres burned in the highway at Doupnitsa 60 kms (35 miles) south of Sofia.
Kostov warned the Socialists that similar disruptions would sweep Bulgaria next week if they voted in a new cabinet instead of calling elections.
"The Socialists should consider this an example of what will happen if they pass a government through parliament," he said. "The Doupnitsa road and rail blockades will become nationwide actions."
